To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
intestinal venous plasma from cats subjected to intestinal shock for 3 hours depresses the myocardium of the cat and rabbit.

intestinal venous blood obtained from cats subjected to intestinal hypotension during activation of vascular constrictor nerve fibers causes a decrease in myocardial contractility of the rabbit papillary muscles and of the isolated perfused rat heart.
the feline small intestine in shock releases into the blood material that causes a significant decrease in myocardial contractility.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of shock in the cat.
the effects of intestinal hypotension on intestinal and systemic hemodynamics.
the cardiovascular effects of the intestinal circulation in shock.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the intestine in shock releases a substance(s) that exerts a depressant effect on the cardiovascular system.
blood-borne cardiocirculatory effects are present in the “shocked small intestine” and that these effects are probably caused by a blood-borne depressant substance.
the feline small intestine in shock releases into blood a material which causes a pronounced depression of myocardial function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the intestine in shock releases a substance(s) into blood that exer-tes a depressant effect on myocardial contractility.
the feline small intestine releases material during simulated shock that depresses cardiovascular function.
the feline small intestine in shock releases a cardiodepressant material into blood that may be responsible for the pronounced derangement in myocardial function observed during intestinal shock.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to induce shock in the small intestine of cats by means of regional hypotension and activation of vaso- and neurogenic mechanisms.
